title: From Water to Cities
learning_goal: Explain how managed river water can support farming and other work, then apply the chain to a different river setting.

sources.title: The Met: First Cities
sources.supports: Southern Mesopotamian irrigation, damaging floods, cities and exchange networks.

sources.title: Spurlock Museum: Mesopotamia
sources.supports: River water, irrigation, transport and alluvial soil.

sources.title: UCL: Egyptian farming
sources.supports: Historical late-summer inundation and autumn planting before modern dams.

steps.title: Water is a resource. People make it useful.
steps.time_context: Urban growth c. 3500–2000 BCE; modern imagery
steps.question: Compare the cyan river area with the amber dry-land area. Why could river access support larger settlements? Explain a connection beyond drinking water.
steps.narration: We are looking at modern Iraq to discuss ancient Mesopotamia. Cyan and amber are schematic comparison areas, not ancient boundaries. How could access to river water help a settlement grow beyond its drinking-water needs?
steps.follow_up: How could getting water to crops change the amount of food available to a settlement?
steps.visual_note: Modern imagery. Coloured rings are teaching highlights, not measured boundaries. Any canal/field shapes are schematic.
hints: Consider how farmers could water crops when local rain was insufficient.
Connect irrigation to extra food, then consider people doing other work.

rubric.expected: River water could be managed for farming; extra food could support non-farming work and exchange. Human organisation mattered too.
reasoning: Connects extra food to other work or exchange.
Recognises that resources require human management.
misconceptions: Floods are always safe and beneficial.
Drinking water alone explains urban growth.

explanation.title: 01 / Move water to crops
explanation.text: Farmers used canals to bring river water to fields. Floods could damage land: water management required work and coordination.
explanation.narration: Farmers used canals to bring river water to fields. Floods could damage land: water management required work and coordination. Say next when you are ready.

explanation.title: 02 / Connect food to other work
explanation.text: Extra food could support people doing specialised work. This is a causal teaching model, not a claim that every household followed one pattern.
explanation.narration: Extra food could support people doing specialised work. This is a causal teaching model, not a claim that every household followed one pattern. Say next when you are ready.

explanation.title: 03 / Resources are not destiny
explanation.text: Waterways connected settlements. Irrigation, exchange and institutions helped cities grow; a nearby river alone was not enough.
explanation.narration: Waterways connected settlements. Irrigation, exchange and institutions helped cities grow; a nearby river alone was not enough. Say next when you are ready.

features.label: Illustrative canal / not a historical trace

steps.title: Same mechanism. A different river.
steps.time_context: Ancient farming before modern dams; modern imagery
steps.question: Apply the idea here: before modern dams, Nile floods helped set the farming calendar. If a flood brought too little water, how might that affect crops and people doing other jobs? Explain the chain.
steps.narration: Now apply your reasoning in Egypt. This is modern imagery, not an ancient reconstruction. Before modern dams, Nile floods helped set the farming calendar. If a flood brought too little water, how might that affect crops and people doing other jobs?
steps.follow_up: Start with less water for fields. What could happen to food availability and then to people who depend on farmers?
steps.visual_note: Modern imagery; teaching highlights only. Ancient flood discussion does not describe today’s dam-regulated cycle.
hints: Separate the chain into water, crops, food and people.
If less food is available, consider workers who do not grow their own.

rubric.expected: Less floodwater could reduce crop production, leaving less food to support other work; actual outcomes depend on storage, management and other conditions.
reasoning: Links food availability to non-farming people.
Applies rather than simply repeats the Mesopotamia example.
misconceptions: Ancient and present-day flood cycles are identical.
A river guarantees sufficient food every year.
Only farmers are affected by poor harvests.

explanation.title: 01 / A historical farming calendar
explanation.text: Before modern dams, late-summer inundation shaped the agricultural year; planting followed in autumn. Today’s imagery cannot show that ancient annual cycle.
explanation.narration: Before modern dams, late-summer inundation shaped the agricultural year; planting followed in autumn. Today’s imagery cannot show that ancient annual cycle. Say next when you are ready.

explanation.title: 02 / Test the chain, not a slogan
explanation.text: In this counterfactual, less water could mean less food for farming and non-farming households. Storage and management could change the outcome.
explanation.narration: In this counterfactual, less water could mean less food for farming and non-farming households. Storage and management could change the outcome. Say next when you are ready.
